newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament declares amnesty for Chechens.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament declares amnesty for Chechens.

text.p: The Russian parliament voted overwhelmingly on Friday to declare an amnesty for Chechens and others who took part in the region's 21-month secessionist war against Russian forces.

The State Duma lower house, dominated by President Boris Yeltsin's communist opponents, backed the amnesty by 235 votes to 39. The measure, which is in line with government policy, was proposed by several opposition-led committees.
Duma officials said the amnesty declaration, in the form of a "parliamentary resolution", had the force of law.
Its main aim is to win the release of Russian prisoners-of-war by exchanging them for Chechens in detention.

The house voted by 228 to nil for a second resolution giving the presidential committee responsible for prisoner exchanges carte blanche to release Chechens from Russian prisons in cases where this would win the freedom of captive Russians.

The measure does not extend to foreigners. A number of volunteers from Moslem countries fought on the Chechen side as did some anti-Russian fighters from former Soviet republics, including Ukraine and the Baltic states.

It did appear to cover those Chechen fighters who staged bloody hostage-taking raids outside the region, in Budyennovsk, Kizlyar and Pervomaiskoye, since it applies to acts committed in areas neighbouring Chechnya. However, those previously classed as dangerous repeat offenders would not be amnestied.
As for Russian servicemen, it does not apply to those who gave weapons to the Chechens, leaving in some doubt the status of soldiers suspected of desertion and still living in Chechnya.
Ultra-nationalist leader Vladimir Zhirinovsky spoke angrily against the whole proposal.

He said it would amnesty "the criminals in the Kremlin who started the war", "cowards" in the army "who threw away their rifles" and Chechen "hardened criminals" languishing in Russian jails for committing "thousands of murders".

There are no accurate figures, but both sides in the conflict say the other is holding hundreds, perhaps thousands, of prisoners. Their exchange, agreed in August's ceasefire, is one of the trickiest issues in continuing peace negotiations.
Moscow accuses the Chechens of seeking freedom for common criminals. The Chechen separatists accuse Russia of classifying its guerrilla fighters as criminals in Russian jails.

Confusing the issue is the fact that considerable numbers of Russian servicemen still in Chechnya following the withdrawal of all remaining troops in January are accused by the Russian military authorities of being fugitive deserters.
